def: The central bright spot of the diffraction pattern of a point source through a circular aperture; radius 0.61λ/NA.
Pinhole diameter equal to the Airy disc diameter, 1.22λ/NA in the sample. One AU balances sectioning and signal.
False low-frequency patterns created when an image is sampled with pixels too large for its finest detail.
Objective corrected for chromatic aberration at three or more wavelengths and spherical aberration at two or more.
Fluorescence from endogenous molecules (NADH, flavins, lipofuscin, collagen); a background, or the signal itself in label-free FLIM.
Plane behind the objective where each direction of light in the sample is focused to one point: a Fourier plane.
A beam with a narrow, long non-diffracting core surrounded by rings, made with an annular pupil.
Combining adjacent pixels into one to gain signal per pixel and speed at the cost of sampling.
Different refractive indices for different polarizations, shown by ordered structures such as spindles, collagen and crystals.
Signal from one fluorophore detected in another's channel because spectra overlap.
Making tissue transparent by matching refractive indices and removing lipids (e.g. CLARITY, iDISCO, CUBIC).
Distance over which a light wave keeps a fixed phase relationship; short coherence gives OCT its depth resolution.
In TEM, how phase contrast at each spatial frequency depends on defocus and aberrations; it oscillates and must be corrected.
Ring on an objective that moves internal lenses to compensate for coverslip thickness or sample index.
Angle of incidence above which light is totally internally reflected: arcsin(n2/n1).
Electrons generated thermally in a sensor without light; reduced by cooling.
Computational reversal of PSF blurring using a measured or modelled PSF.
Axial range over which the specimen appears in focus; shrinks with higher NA.
Interference filter at 45° that reflects some wavelengths and transmits others, separating excitation from emission.
Removing stage or sample movement over time, using fiducial beads or image cross-correlation.
Fraction of time a switching fluorophore spends in its on state; low duty cycles are needed for dense SMLM labelling.
On-chip avalanche amplification in an EMCCD that lifts signals above read noise.
Illumination through the objective, so the same lens excites and collects; the standard fluorescence geometry.
A non-propagating field that decays exponentially beyond a totally reflecting interface; excites a ~100 nm layer in TIRF.
Extra noise from stochastic gain (√2 for EMCCDs), equivalent to halving quantum efficiency.
How strongly a molecule absorbs at a wavelength (M⁻¹cm⁻¹).
A bright, stable bead or particle used to register channels or correct drift.
Diameter (mm) of the intermediate image field an eyepiece or port can use; field of view = FN / magnification.
Average time a fluorophore stays excited before emitting, typically 1-5 ns; sensitive to its environment.
Donor-acceptor distance at which FRET efficiency is 50%, typically 4-7 nm.
Resolution estimate from the correlation of two independent half-images across spatial frequencies.
A fast motor-driven mirror that steers the beam in point-scanning microscopes.
Photomultiplier with gallium arsenide phosphide photocathode, about 40-45% QE in the visible.
Detector combining a photocathode with an avalanche diode for high QE, low noise and photon counting.
Liquid between objective and coverslip (oil, water, glycerol, silicone) that sets the maximum NA.
Region over which an aberration correction stays valid, often only tens of µm in tissue.
Illumination scheme giving even light with the lamp imaged into the condenser aperture, not the specimen.
Uncertainty in the fitted position of a single emitter, roughly PSF σ/√N.
Region of the 3D widefield OTF with no axial information, the reason widefield cannot section.
Directions not sampled in tomography because the specimen cannot tilt beyond about ±60-70°.
Contrast transmitted at each spatial frequency; the modulus of the OTF.
Spinning disk with a spiral of pinholes that scans many foci in parallel.
Sampling at least twice the highest spatial frequency present; pixels ≤ λ/4NA at the sample.
Thin slice of a thick sample imaged without out-of-focus light.
Fourier transform of the PSF; describes how each spatial frequency is transferred by the optics.
Light-driven switching of a fluorophore from dark to bright or one colour to another (PA-GFP, mEos).
Irreversible destruction of a fluorophore by light, often via the triplet state and oxygen.
Damage to living samples by illumination, often through reactive oxygen species.
Aperture in an image plane that blocks out-of-focus light in confocal microscopes.
Image of a point source; the 'blur kernel' of the microscope.
Fraction of photons a detector converts into signal.
Fraction of absorbed photons re-emitted as fluorescence.
Two points are resolved when the peak of one falls on the first minimum of the other: d = 0.61λ/NA.
Distance from a Gaussian beam waist over which the beam area doubles; half the usable light-sheet length.
Electronic noise added when a pixel is read out, in electrons RMS.
Ratio of light speed in vacuum to that in a medium; mismatches cause aberration.
Scientific CMOS camera: low read noise, high speed and large field, with per-pixel amplifiers.
Statistical fluctuation in photon counts, √N; the fundamental noise floor.
Device that shapes light's phase or amplitude pixel by pixel, used for SIM, lattices and adaptive optics.
Separating overlapping fluorophores by fitting each pixel's spectrum to reference spectra.
Difference between excitation and emission peak wavelengths.
Peak intensity of the real PSF relative to a perfect one; ≥0.8 is diffraction limited.
Complete reflection of light hitting a lower-index medium beyond the critical angle.
Lens forming the image from an infinity-corrected objective; its focal length sets magnification.
Non-crystalline ice formed by plunge freezing, preserving specimens for cryo-EM.
Gap between the objective front lens and the coverslip or sample when in focus.
Screening assay quality measure from control means and standard deviations; >0.5 is excellent.
